The story is tightly woven, with every detail contributing to the quiet emotional tension between Ilse and her son, Jonas. The beginning establishes the contrast between Ilse's rugged, traditional life on the ferry and Jonas's out-of-place, exhausted city demeanor (his thin coat, muddy leather shoes, and analytical gaze). The middle builds on this distance through their sparse dialogue about the dying ferry business, revealing Ilse's stubborn attachment to her routine and Jonas's pragmatic skepticism. This logically and satisfyingly leads to the ending: when Ilse notices how cold and tense her son is, she breaks her strict adherence to her work schedule—closing the ferry early despite her earlier insistence that the schoolkids would be coming—to take him home and make tea. Every sensory detail and action serves this subtle, unspoken gesture of maternal care and reconciliation.
